title: Thankfulness and the Craving Graves
speaker: Elder Jim Blizzard
summary: This sermon examines Numbers 11 and the story of Israel's craving for meat in the wilderness, where God judged their discontentment by giving them exactly what they demanded. Elder Blizzard contrasts a thankful heart that humbly receives God's provision with a proud heart that complains it deserves more, showing how thanklessness is rooted in pride and how Christ alone can truly satisfy our deepest hungers.

outline.title: A Thankless Heart Forgets What God Has Given
subpoints: Israel remembered Egypt falsely, recalling only the food while forgetting the slavery and bondage
Discontentment has a terrible memory that edits the past to make sin look better than God's mercy
The problem was not wanting food but craving the gift more than the Giver
We become blind to God's ordinary mercies through taking blessings for granted
Cultivate a discipline of noticing three specific mercies from God daily

outline.title: A Proud Heart Demands What God Has Withheld
subpoints: A desire becomes a demand when we are willing to sin to get it and believe God is not good without it
God gave Israel exactly what they craved as judgment to expose their idolatry
Kibroth Hatava—the graves of craving—shows that discontentment digs its own grave
God's withholding is often wisdom and protection, not neglect
Complaining is sin, not a personality quirk, and is the seed that grows into rebellion

outline.title: Thanklessness Is Rooted in Pride
subpoints: A thankful heart says 'I have received more than I deserve'; a proud heart says 'I deserve more than I received'
Refusal to give thanks is a declaration that the creature deserves better from the Creator
Biblical lament differs from sinful complaining: lament trusts God while complaining judges God
A lament says 'Lord, this hurts but I trust you'; complaining says 'Lord, you have failed me'
Complaining places us in the judge's seat over God's providence

outline.title: Christ Is Our True Bread and Complete Satisfaction
subpoints: Jesus contrasts himself with the manna generation: the manna could fill stomachs but not satisfy souls
Manna could not change hearts or give eternal life, but Christ is the true bread from heaven
Israel craved and fell; Christ trusted and conquered in the wilderness
Christ died for proud, craving, complaining, and entitled hearts
In Christ we have forgiveness, grace to desire what is holy, and contentment in all circumstances

outline.title: Receiving God's No as Fatherly Wisdom
subpoints: God's withholding is often a mercy and protection, like a loving parent preventing spoiled appetite
A closed door may be protection; a delayed answer may be training
Hard providence in the wilderness teaches us to hunger for Christ above all else
Every desire must bow before God; pray 'if this desire honors you, purify it; if it rules me, kill it'
We need to align our desires with God's and see his refusals as fatherly wisdom

outline.title: Cultivating a Grateful Home and Grateful Hearts
subpoints: Homes can be gardens of gratitude or greenhouses for grumbling
Fathers should model trusting God more than complaining about circumstances
Mothers must resist comparison that kills gratitude
Children learn to receive ordinary blessings with joy; grandparents pass down stories of God's faithfulness
Gratitude gives us a steady heart in hard providences by remembering past mercies

outline.title: From the Graves of Craving to the Table of Grace
subpoints: A full stomach with an empty soul is a tragedy; a satisfied heart in Christ is true abundance
The issue is not whether our hands are full but whether our heart is satisfied in our Savior
Christ offers himself as a better feast—one that truly satisfies and never spoils
True thankfulness begins when we can say 'Father, because I have Christ, I have more than I deserve'
One with Christ as the bread of life possesses that which truly satisfies, even amidst earthly deprivation

transcript:
## Reading of God's Word

> "Now when the people complained, it displeased the Lord. For the Lord heard it and his anger was aroused, so the fire of the Lord burned among them and consumed some in the outskirts of the camp. Then the people cried out to Moses and when Moses prayed to the Lord, the fire was quenched. So he called the name of that place Taberah because the fire of the Lord had burned among them. Now the mixed multitude who were among them yielded to intense craving. So the children of Israel also wept again and said, Who will give us meat to eat? We remember the fish which we ate freely in Egypt, the cucumbers, the melons, the leeks, the onions, and the garlic. But now our whole being is dried up. There's nothing at all except this manna before our eyes. Now the manna was like coriander seed and its color like the color of bdellium. The people went out and gathered it, ground it on millstones, or beat it in the mortar, cooked it in pans and made cakes of it. And its taste was like the taste of pastry prepared with oil. And when the dew fell on the camp in the night, the manna fell on it." (Numbers 11:1-8)

> "Now a wind went out from the Lord and it brought quail from the sea and left them fluttering near the camp about a day's journey on this side and about a day's journey on the other side all around the camp and about two cubits above the surface of the ground. And the people stayed up all day, all night, and all the next day and gathered the quail. One man gathered ten homers and they spread them out for themselves all around the camp. But while the meat was still between their teeth before it was chewed, the wrath of the Lord was aroused against the people and the Lord struck the people with a very great plague. So he called the name of that place Kibroth Hattaavah because there they buried the people who had yielded to craving. From Kibroth Hattaavah the people moved to Hazaroth and camped at Hazaroth." (Numbers 11:31-34)

Greetings to you from the Grace Bible Presbyterian Church in Cape Canaveral, Florida. We are your brothers and sisters in Christ and we join with you in worship even today.

## Thanksgiving as a Christian Grace

This morning, as I was thinking about this passage, we often celebrate Thanksgiving one time a year, often in November. But it's not just a seasonal virtue. Thanksgiving is a Christian grace. A thankful heart says, "Lord, I have received more than I deserve." But a proud heart will say, "Lord, I deserve more than I've received."

Numbers 11 brings us to one of the most sobering scenes in Israel's wilderness journey. God had redeemed the people from Egypt. He had brought them through the Red Sea. He had guided them by cloud and fire. He had fed them daily bread from heaven. And yet the very place where they should have been learning trust, they began to crave what God had not given them.

The name of the place tells the story. Kibroth Hattaavah—the graves of craving. Israel received what they demanded there, but their feast became a funeral.

> "He gave them their request but sent leanness into their soul." (Psalm 106:15)

That is the warning before us. A proud heart may receive what it demands and still lose what it needs most. And so today we consider this truth: a thankful heart humbly receives what God has given, but a proud heart complains, "I've not received enough."

## A Thankless Heart Forgets What God Has Given

Numbers 11 describes this day when God's people got exactly what they wanted and died because of it. Israel had all they needed. God had redeemed them from Egypt. They had this daily provision of manna. God had guided them personally. They were promised a land flowing with milk and honey. And yet in verse four they murmur and complain.

> "Now the mixed multitude who were among them yielded to intense craving. So the children of Israel wept again and said, 'Who will give us meat to eat? We remember the fish which we ate freely in Egypt, the cucumbers, the melons, the leeks, the onions, the garlic. But now our whole being is dried up and there is nothing at all except this manna before our eyes.'" (Numbers 11:4-6)

They remembered Egypt, but they remembered it wrong. They remembered it falsely. They say, "We remember the fish we got for free." Yes, free with every beating, free with every brick quota, free with every slavery that you have. They also list these other things that are missing: the cucumbers, the leeks, the melons, onions, and garlic. They say they had these things freely. But they don't remember the slavery. They don't remember the brick quotas. They don't remember the cruelty of Pharaoh. They don't remember crying out under bondage.

You see, discontentment has a terrible memory. It remembers the flavors of Egypt, but it forgets the chains. It remembers the fish, but it forgets the slavery. It remembers the cucumbers and melons, but forgets the whip. That's what complaining does in our own lives. It edits the past so that sin looks better than God's mercy.

What they're actually doing here is rejecting God's provision, God's presence, God's wisdom, God's goodness. What they wanted instead was meat like they had back in Egypt. They wanted comfort without faith. They wanted the blessings without obedience. This is the heart of the problem. They were not thankful for what God had given. They were not satisfied with God himself.

The problem wasn't that they wanted food. God himself had given them manna. The problem is that they craved the gift more than the Giver and wanted even more. Thankfulness is ruined when our hearts crave the gift more than the God who gives it—whether that gift is comfort or recognition, success or ease, security, pleasure, or control.

Today we come to the graves of craving to learn how to cultivate a humble and thankful heart. We need to work to cultivate a discipline of noticing God's daily mercies.

> "Daily God loads us with benefits." (Psalm 68)

The manna that the Israelites were receiving wasn't flashy, but it was faithful. It wasn't luxurious, but it was miraculous. Every morning Israel woke up to a visible proof that God had not forgotten them. The ground every morning preached a sermon: "The Lord provides." But instead of seeing it as a daily mercy, they saw it as a daily monotony. "We got to gather it again."

One of the reasons we complain is not that God has been inactive, but that we have become blind to His ordinary mercies. We stop being amazed that there's food on our table every day, that He's provided work for us to provide for our families, that there is breath in our lungs. How many of you have thought about breathing this morning and yet God has provided that for you? That we have Scripture in our hands, the very word of God. We have a church to gather with. We have forgiveness in Christ. We have grace for another day.

The problem is not that God has been stingy. The problem is that we have stopped seeing the things that God has given to us. Thankfulness dies when we take blessings for granted.

### Practicing Daily Gratitude

Begin today. Think of three mercies that God has already given you—not vague blessings, but specific evidences of His kindness. A conversation that encouraged you, a warm meal, a Scripture that God used at the right time, a moment of grace. Watch your gratitude grow and then do it tomorrow and the next day and the next. Not as a rote exercise, but as a way of training your heart to see even the small mercies that God has provided.

## A Proud Heart Demands What God Has Withheld

You see, a proud heart demands what God has withheld. The sin of the Israelites isn't that they wanted meat. God is not against food. God is not against physical enjoyment. God had already provided food for them. The issue was that the desire became a demand. They were no longer asking as dependent children. They were grumbling as entitled judges.

### When Desire Becomes Idolatry

How do you know when a desire becomes a demand? It's when you are willing to sin in order to get it. When you can't thank God without that thing. When you believe God is not good unless He gives it. That's idolatry—putting something before God. When your peace depends on having it. When in your heart you say, "I cannot be content unless God does this my way."

And so God gave them what they wanted. He says, "You want meat? Okay, I'll give you meat."

> "You shall eat not one day, nor two, nor five, nor 10, nor 20. For a whole month until it comes out your nostrils and becomes loathsome to you, because you have despised the Lord who is among you and have wept before him saying, 'Why did we ever come up out of Egypt?'" (Numbers 11:19-20)

This isn't petty anger on the part of God. This is judgment designed to expose the idolatry of the people. And so we come to the place of judgment. The name Kibroth Hattaavah literally means "graves of craving," tombs literally dug because of the lust of the people. The message is absolutely unforgettable: discontentment digs its own grave.

> "He gave them what they asked but sent leanness into their soul." (Psalm 106:15)

The idea here is that leanness is a spiritual emptiness, the hollowness that comes from indulging in desire without repentance. This is a terrifying verse. He gave them what they asked but sent leanness into their soul. It means that there are times when the answer we demand from God is the very thing that exposes us.

### God's No Is a Mercy

Sometimes God's no is actually a mercy. Sometimes God withholding things from us is a protection. Sometimes we think we cannot live without this thing, but it would actually ruin us if God were to give it. The Israelites got their meat. They got their craving and it ruined them.

I see children here. How many of you have ever had your child ask you for candy or ice cream before dinner? I imagine having ice cream and candy is not evil, right? But a loving father, a loving mother will often tell their child, "Not before dinner. Not now. We don't want to spoil your appetite." And yet the child often thinks, "Well, if my father loved me, he'd give it to me now."

Israel looked at God's withholding and said, "This is neglect. God's not caring for us." When in fact God's withholding the thing was actually wisdom. The greatest judgment God may give is not drought or famine or hardship but to hand us over to our own desires.

> "God gave them over to uncleanness... they dishonor their bodies." (Romans 1)

We need to repent of the sin of complaining. Complaining is not a personality glitch. Scripture says that it's sin.

> "Do all things without murmuring, without complaining." (Philippians 2)

In Numbers 11, complaint is the seed that grows into rebellion. God may judge a demanding heart by giving it exactly what it wants. Israel demands meat apart from thankful trust and God let their craving become their judgment.

> "While the meat was still between their teeth before it was chewed, the wrath of the Lord was aroused against the people and the Lord struck the people with a very great plague." (Numbers 11:33)

Their feast became a funeral. Their cravings became graves.

## Thanklessness Is Rooted in Pride

But this leads us to a deeper issue than just the craving. You see, their thanklessness was not weakness. It was really pride. Pride is at the heart of so many sins. A thankful heart is not a proud heart, but a thankless heart is a proud heart.

> "Although they knew God they did not glorify him as God nor were they thankful." (Romans 1)

Paul says the downward spiral of the human spirit, of the human heart, begins with refusing to honor God and to give thanks. That means thanklessness is not small cracks in the walls. It's a foundational problem. When the creature refuses to thank the Creator, he's already trying to live as though his life is his own.

That's why the first question of the Heidelberg Catechism begins where our pride must die: "I am not my own but belong body and soul to my Savior in life and in death, who fully paid for my sins with his precious blood."

The refusal to give thanks is not a trivial sin. It's a declaration that "I deserve better than what God has given me."

In Israel's case their desire became demands. Their demands became complaints. Their complaints became rebellion. And rebellion ended in graves. The root of thanklessness is pride.

We need to say, "Lord, I have received more than I deserved," rather than "Lord, I deserve more than I got."

That's why complaining is not a small thing. Thanklessness is not just sadness. It's not just disappointment. It's not even the same thing as grief. Scripture clearly leaves room for grief. Scripture is full of the language of lament. The Psalms are full of honest cries to God. But complaining is different.

### Lament vs. Complaining

A biblical lament shows sorrow to God in faith, but sinful complaining places us above God as the judge. A lament says, "Lord, this hurts but I trust you." Complaining says, "Lord, this is wrong and I accuse you of it."

A lament will say, "I go to God with my pain." Complaining pulls away from God in pride.

A lament says, "How long, O Lord?" A complaint will say, "Why have you failed me?"

Complaining puts me in the judge's seat over the providence of God. It says, "God, your provision is not enough. Your timing is not wise enough. Your way is not good enough."

That was Israel's sin. They didn't merely want meat. They wanted to overrule what God had said.

A thankful heart will receive life as a gift while a proud heart will treat life as payment, as the wages. A thankful heart will say, "Everything good comes from the Lord." A proud heart will say, "I should have had more by now."

Ask God to shape your cravings, to shape your heart, not just to satisfy them. Ask God to give you the desires that will honor him.

> "Incline my heart to your testimonies and not to covetousness." (Psalm 119)

## Christ Is Our True Bread and Complete Satisfaction

Honestly, the answer to this is Christ. In the New Testament we see that Christ is our true bread.

> "Your fathers ate manna in the wilderness and are dead." (John 6)

Many of the wilderness generation died under judgment. Numbers 11 gives us one of these vivid scenes.

> "So he called the name of that place Kibroth Hattaavah because there they buried the people who had yielded to craving." (Numbers 11:34)

Jesus in John chapter 6 says:

> "I am the bread of life. He who comes to me shall never hunger." (John 6)

You see, the idea is not that the people in Numbers 11 died from eating the manna because the manna couldn't give them eternal life. Though the manna was a real gift from God, it kept bodies alive in the wilderness. But manna could not change their heart. Manna could fill their stomachs but it could not satisfy their soul.

Israel's problem wasn't that they had empty hands. Their problem was a craving heart. And so Jesus says that the true bread is ultimately not something that God drops from heaven. It's someone that God sent from heaven.

Israel grumbled in the wilderness but Christ obeyed in the wilderness. Israel demanded bread but Jesus fasted and trusted his Father. Israel said, "Has God given us enough yet?" And Jesus says:

> "Man shall not live by bread alone but by every word that comes from the mouth of God." (Matthew 4)

You see, Israel craved and fell, but Christ trusted and conquered. Jesus here is contrasting that real temporary provision of manna with himself, the true bread from heaven, the only one who can give eternal life.

Christ is not merely our example of contentment. He is our Savior from sins—including thanklessness. He died for proud hearts, for craving hearts, for complaining hearts, for entitled hearts. He bore the judgment his people deserved so that the graves of craving would not have its final word over us.

Christ has given us a heart satisfied in him. Forgiveness for a thankful or thankless spirit. Grace to desire what is holy. Contentment in all our circumstances.

> "In whatever circumstance I've found myself, in that place I have learned to be content." (Philippians 4, Paul)

We need to align our desires with God's. We need to submit our desires to God. It's not wrong to desire necessarily, but every desire must bow before our Lord and Maker. Pray: "Lord, if this desire honors you, purify it. But if it rules me, kill it."

## Receiving God's No as Fatherly Wisdom

We need to see God's no as fatherly wisdom. We need to receive his withholding as a mercy. When God does not give us one of the things we think we need, his refusal is mercy. That closed door may actually be a protection. A delayed answer may be his training. A hard providence in the wilderness where God teaches us to hunger for Christ.

We are to eat by faith of the true bread. We need to feed on Christ by faith. Discontentment will say, "I need more," but our faith should answer, "I have all I need. I have Christ."

And that will not make every sorrow disappear, but it will give the soul an anchor deeper than our circumstances.

## A Grateful Home and Grateful Hearts

This needs to begin in our homes. Our homes can either be gardens of gratitude or greenhouses for grumbling.

Fathers, your family should hear you trust God more than complain about the circumstances. Mothers, you need to resist the comparison that kills gratitude. Children, learn to receive ordinary blessings with joy. Grandparents, tell the next generation of what God has done, how he has been faithful.

A thankful home is not something that happens by accident. It grows where God's mercies are noticed, where they're named, and where they're received with humility. Gratitude gives us a steady heart in hard providences. When we remember God's past mercies we are better prepared to trust him in the present trials.

Everything God gives is for our good even if it's not what we wanted. The wilderness should teach us to want God more than his gifts. Israel wanted meat more than they wanted God.

> "While the meat was still between their teeth before it was chewed, the wrath of the Lord was aroused against the people and the Lord struck the people with a very great plague." (Numbers 11:33)

Their feast became a funeral. Their cravings became graves. But the gospel gives us a better feast.

## From the Graves of Craving to the Table of Grace

> "I am the bread of life. Whoever comes to me shall not hunger." (John 6)

Christ offers himself as that better feast—a feast that satisfies truly, a feast that will never spoil, a feast that never becomes judgment for those who believe.

True thankfulness begins when we can say, "Father, because I have Christ, I have more than I deserve and more than I can lose."

The issue is not if our hands are full. It's whether our heart is satisfied in our Savior. We may have every earthly comfort and still possess a lean soul. But the one who has Christ as the bread of life has that which truly satisfies.

Most of you when we finish here will eat something this afternoon, I imagine. Don't leave the table with a full stomach and an empty soul. Instead, let us leave with full hearts, feasting on the goodness of our Savior.

So today let us leave the graves of craving and come by faith to the table of grace. God has given us more than enough.
